graphlearnR

graphlearnR is a framework for machine learning on graphs and graph neural networks in R. It is built on the torch package, so models run on the CPU or a GPU, and nothing calls Python.

It covers the whole workflow: validated graph data with explicit 1-based indexing, conversion from igraph, edge lists and sparse matrices, message passing layers, neighbor sampling, leakage safe splits, training for node, edge, link and graph level tasks, evaluation, heterogeneous and temporal graphs, graph transformers, and explanations.

Installation 

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("adamrsophie/graphlearnR")

# LibTorch, once per machine
torch::install_torch()

Example 

library(graphlearnR)

g <- dataset_karate()                       # Zachary's karate club
g <- split_nodes(g, seed = 42)              # stratified train, val, test masks

model <- gnn_model("sage", input_dim = 34, hidden_dim = 16, output_dim = 2)
fit <- train_graph_model(model, g, task = "node_classification",
                         epochs = 150, early_stopping = 20, seed = 1)

evaluate_graph_model(fit, g)                # accuracy, F1, AUC, calibration
head(predict(fit, g))                       # one row per node

Graph classification and link prediction use the same interface:

graphs <- dataset_synthetic_graphs(120, seed = 1)
gin <- gnn_model("gin", 1, 32, 2, pool = "sum")
fit_g <- train_graph_model(gin, graphs, "graph_classification", batch_size = 16)

split <- split_edges(dataset_sbm(c(50, 50), seed = 1), seed = 1)
fit_l <- train_graph_model(gnn_model("gcn", 8, 32), split, "link_prediction")
evaluate_graph_model(fit_l)                 # AUC, AP, MRR, Hits@k

Features

Area What is included
Graph data graph_data() with node, edge and graph features and labels, weights, masks, identifiers; undirected pairs stored in both directions; validation with clear errors
Conversion igraph, edge lists with arbitrary identifiers, dense and sparse adjacency matrices, torch tensors on any device
Batching graph_batch() and unbatch(), lazy and on disk datasets, transforms
Message passing vectorized scatter sum, mean, max, min, std, softmax; a general message_passing() for custom layers
Layers GraphSAGE, GCN, GraphConv, GIN and GINE, GAT, GATv2, transformer convolution, NNConv, RGCN; global and top-k pooling
Training node, edge, link and graph classification and regression; full batch or neighbor sampled; early stopping, schedulers, checkpoints, reproducibility record
Splits stratified node splits, link splits without leakage, edge label, group, scaffold and temporal splits; negative sampling
Heterogeneous graphs typed nodes and relations, reverse relations, typed sampling, relation specific link splits, heterogeneous GNNs
Temporal graphs event streams, causal neighborhoods, snapshots, graph GRU, spatiotemporal forecasting, dynamic link prediction with baselines
Graph transformers Laplacian and random walk encodings, shortest path distances, Graphormer style model
Explainability saliency, integrated gradients, edge gradients, occlusion, GNNExplainer, attention weights, fidelity and stability
Datasets karate club, stochastic block models, synthetic graph, heterogeneous and temporal data; checksum verified downloaders for TU and LINQS datasets

Conventions

  • Indices are 1-based in every interface: edge_index, seeds, pairs, returned node ids. to_zero_based() converts at an explicit boundary.
  • Edges point from source to target; layers aggregate incoming edges.
  • Undirected graphs are given once per pair and stored in both directions; edge_pair links the two directions, and splits and samplers respect it.
  • Functions that draw random numbers take a seed and leave the caller’s random number stream untouched.

Documentation

The package website has a reference for every function and articles on graph data, message passing, each task, sampling, heterogeneous and temporal graphs, graph transformers, explainability, and evaluation.

How it is tested

Every layer is checked for permutation equivariance, against a dense or reference formula, and with finite difference gradients in double precision. Pooled models are checked for permutation invariance and batched forward passes against separate ones. Splits, samplers and temporal code are checked for leakage. Continuous integration runs R CMD check on Linux, macOS and Windows.

Related work

graphlearnR follows the layer designs of PyTorch Geometric (Fey and Lenssen 2019). In R, igraph and tidygraph cover graph analysis and manipulation, and graphlearnR converts from both. It is part of a series of R packages by the same author with symcompR and z3r.
